reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the conflict diachronically: Jacob's double marriage predates Sinai, so no law yet existed to break, and Leviticus 18:18 legislates against precisely the rivalry his case produced.

discrepancy.connective: Source critic Steven DiMattei presses the sharpest objection: the conflict is not a timing gap but two authors — the Yahwist's Genesis 29, where marrying sisters is unremarked, against the Priestly Leviticus centuries later, which condemns it.

skeptic.name: Steven DiMattei
skeptic.work: Contradictions in the Bible #50, "Is it lawful to marry your wife's sister OR not? (Gen 29:28 vs Lev 18:18)"
skeptic.attribution: Dr. Steven DiMattei, Contradictions in the Bible #50 (contradictionsinthebible.com, 2013)

excerpts.excerpt_text: This bigamy of Jacob must not be judged directly by the Mosaic law, which prohibits marriage with two sisters at the same time (Lev 18:18), or set down as incest (Calvin, etc.), since there was no positive law on the point in existence then.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly names Lev 18:18 and resolves the tension by chronology — no positive law existed when Jacob married, so the patriarchal marriage cannot be Torah-illegal. The strongest single reconcile on the row.

excerpts.excerpt_text: It is evident that the marriage of both sisters took place nearly about the same time, and that such a connection was then allowed, though afterwards prohibited (Lev 18:18).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly states the diachronic-development harmonization: the sister-marriage was allowed in Jacob's day, prohibited only later by Lev 18:18. Distinct voice, concise.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Connections of this kind are now called incestuous; but it appears they were allowable in those ancient times. … It was probably because of this that the law was made, Thou shalt not take a wife to her sister, to vex her, besides the other in her life-time. After this, all such marriages were strictly forbidden.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Adds the causal claim that Jacob's case itself prompted the later prohibition; ellipsis joins the 'allowable then' clause to the 'law made later' clause, preserving Clarke's diachronic argument. Distinct voice.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on Genesis 29:27 (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: Treats this exact pair: argues Jacob's marriage to two sisters cannot be judged by Lev 18:18 because no positive law existed then, and that the case prepared the way for the later prohibition. Row-surfaced harmonizing commentator used per spec because Haley's coverage of this specific pair could not be confirmed.
